channel.title: Deseret News - Faith
channel.description: Faith news and stories from Deseret News

item.title: Illustrated ‘New Testament Stories’ available online and in print
item.description: Children can now read a refreshed New Testament Stories, the Latter-day Saint church's illustrated scripture book, which has revised text and new artwork and comes in print as well as a digital edition. Rosemary K. Chibota, who leads the Primary organization, said "a joyful spirit" runs through the book, which Chibota said grew out of a wish to help children connect with scripture and better understand Jesus Christ.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Why Melissa Dalton-Bradford thinks you should be more political
item.description: Mariya Manzhos profiles Melissa Dalton-Bradford, a Frankfurt-based Latter-day Saint author who co-founded Mormon Women for Ethical Government and turned her Instagram account, now followed by about half a million people, into a civic-engagement platform after watching Zelenskyy's February 2025 Oval Office clash with Trump. In her new book, How to Save Democracy, she uses histories of collapsed democracies to flag warning signs in the U.S. and urges readers to act, for instance by forming a "democracy defense pod," while maintaining that her work is not partisan and that her deepest identity is as a follower of Jesus Christ. Offering a conservative view, Carolyn Phippen of the Women's Republican Club of Salt Lake City argues both parties should reject departures from the Constitution but faults the left for blaming others, while Dalton-Bradford says the real question is whether today's problems can be addressed "without dismantling democracy".
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: Elder Stevenson participates in World Forum of Intercultural Dialogue
item.description: Taking part in the 7th World Forum of Intercultural Dialogue in Baku was a highlight of Elder Gary E. Stevenson's Oct. 22-31 assignment in the Europe Central Area, the Church's Europe Newsroom reported. The apostle also met with civic and religious figures in Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan and with Latter-day Saints there and in Paris and Vienna.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: ‘Luz de las Naciones’ celebrates celestial and ancestral roots
item.description: Around 1,000 volunteers in traditional dress will bring folk music and dance from across Latin America to the Church of Jesus Christ's Conference Center for the 24th annual Luz de las Naciones on Nov. 13 and 14, with Saturday's show streamed live in Spanish and in-person seats sold out apart from a standby line. Elder Jason C. Jensen, the Area Seventy who chairs the show's executive committee, said it is meant for everyone no matter what language they speak, adding, "Jesus Christ is the light of all nations." First-time choreographer Brianna Flores Villaalta replaced the usual Cuban salsa with a caringa courtship dance, saying she wanted "to give more recognition to the Cuban culture".
item.dc:creator: Ariel Harmer

item.title: Jimmer Fredette tells BYU-Hawaii students to make Jesus Christ their Plan A
item.description: In a Tuesday devotional at BYU-Hawaii, Jimmer Fredette described how his childhood goal of reaching the NBA came true when the Sacramento Kings drafted him in 2011, then soured into benchwarming, lost confidence and harsh criticism until Elder M. Russell Ballard reached out and challenged him to read the Book of Mormon every day for the rest of the season. Fredette said the reading lifted his mood even though his playing time didn't change, and he came to treat the Savior rather than basketball as his "Plan A", a focus he carried through later pro stints abroad and onto the 3x3 team at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
item.dc:creator: Krysyan Edler

item.title: Apostle of the Church of Jesus Christ praises Pope Leo’s ‘sincere desire’ for peace
item.description: Elder Ulisses Soares, an apostle of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, was in Buenos Aires on a 10-day South America assignment and attended an interfaith gathering Monday at Palacio San Martín, where Pope Leo XIV, partway through his own 12-day trip, told religious leaders that all "religions safeguard human dignity" in his address. Soares said afterward he was impressed by the pope's "sincere desire to invite all people to promote peace in the world." In a social media post, the apostle linked that message to President Dallin H. Oaks' recent appeal for God's children to act as peacemakers by keeping the commandments to love God and neighbor.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Episode 322: Retired Marine Col. Jason Perry speaks about military service, faith and resilience on Veterans Day
item.description: Jason S.D. Perry, who retired as a Marine Corps colonel after a 30-year military career, now leads wargaming at the Naval Postgraduate School; for Veterans Day, Perry joins Church News reporter Mary Richards on the Church News podcast to reflect on serving as a Latter-day Saint in uniform. The conversation covers faith and resilience, the part chaplains and local Church members and leaders play, and advice for young members considering military service.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Trump, God and forgiveness
item.description: Asked by Ross Douthat in a 60 Minutes interview whether he could forgive his political enemies if his own entry into heaven depended on it, President Donald Trump answered that he "probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will". Manzhos notes the exchange came a week after Republicans' midterm losses, as white evangelicals and born-again Christians, who backed Trump at about 82% in each of his three presidential runs, slipped from 23% of 2024 voters to 17% in this midterm, and cites Mark Tooley, president of the Institute on Religion & Democracy, who wrote in The Dispatch that "MAGA Christianity will end" as evangelicals face a post-Trump era. The newsletter also covers Bob Dylan's brief Vatican meeting with Pope Leo and a new documentary on Utah's soda culture.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: A refreshed youth program reveals Latter-day Saint leaders’ hopes for the next generation
item.description: Believe, belong and become anchor the three new aims of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints' Children and Youth program, announced Nov. 3 with adjustments that take effect in January 2027. Youth will pick or write their own monthly invitation tied to their For the Strength of Youth lessons and children ages 8 to 11 will set one monthly goal, replacing the current four-area goal structure, while new milestone events and monthly lessons on becoming covenant sons and daughters of God round out the changes. Primary General President Rosemary K. Chibota said the program's purpose has not changed, and Sister Tamara W. Runia of the Young Women general presidency said "Traditions alone will not be enough" to sustain youth once they leave home.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Counterprotesters overwhelm activists targeting Jewish businesses Sunday
item.description: A bicycle "boycott ride" targeting six Jewish businesses in Philadelphia's Rittenhouse Square on Sunday was outnumbered by hundreds of counterprotesters, who at times formed a wall between the dozens of riders and the restaurants. Police made three arrests, and all six eateries drew long lunchtime lines, with Mac Mart owner Marti Lieberman saying she was "totally overwhelmed" by supporters of every background. Lieberman, who suspects she was singled out because her social media videos show her wearing a Star of David, said she has never mixed religion or politics with her business, while the organizers dismissed any suggestion of a message in the ride's timing, which coincided with the anniversary of Kristallnacht.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Hess

item.title: How a Team USA wrestler grappled with the choice to serve a Latter-day Saint mission
item.description: Team USA wrestler Alex Hedrick stepped away from her sport at 25 to serve a Latter-day Saint mission in New York after placing third at the 2024 Olympic trials, a decision she says became "so clear" to her through prayer. Being six or seven years older than most of her fellow missionaries was a hard adjustment at first, but her mission leaders said her maturity made her a steadying presence, and she kept training on whatever equipment she could find, including wrestling mats at a meetinghouse in her final area. Now back on Team USA with a Grand View Open title and a top-three national ranking, Hedrick is aiming for the 2028 Los Angeles Games and says her mission taught her "I need to be able to be on a team".
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen

item.title: How an artist painted the rotunda of this historic ward house in Cody, Wyoming
item.description: The dome of Cody, Wyoming's first Latter-day Saint meetinghouse carries a mural of Church history by Edward T. Grigware, a painter who never joined the faith but agreed to the project after local members approached him in the late 1940s. Grigware prepared for close to a year, reading up on the Church's past and traveling to several of its historic sites, before covering the rotunda's 36-foot-diameter ceiling.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: New ASL Sunday School presidency serves deaf and hard-of-hearing Church members
item.description: Deaf and hard-of-hearing Latter-day Saints in the United States now have their own ASL Sunday School presidency, which oversees video-based adult religion instruction offered in sign language nationwide. Its president, Marriner Merrill, said the group's aims are those of any Sunday School, from "getting to know our students" to "teaching the gospel in the Savior's way".
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Planned Sunday boycott of Jewish-owned businesses in Philadelphia sparks condemnation
item.description: A Sunday bike rally by the activist group Philly Bike On Your Left, aimed at six Jewish-owned businesses at Philadelphia's Rittenhouse Square under a flyer reading "No business for Zionists" and set for the eve of the Kristallnacht anniversary, has drawn swift condemnation from Pennsylvania officials and national leaders. Gov. Josh Shapiro called the ride "nothing more than blatant antisemitism designed to intimidate" and drive Jewish businesses out, and Mayor Cherelle Parker said singling out owners for being Jewish is unacceptable while affirming the rights of peaceful demonstrators. The group did not respond to media requests but posted a video defending the boycott and denying any deliberate timing, while Hess cites FBI data showing anti-Jewish hate crimes make up roughly 69% of religiously motivated hate crimes.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Hess

item.title: Learn about the hymn ‘Fight the Good Fight’ in new Latter-day Saint hymnbook
item.description: The hymn Fight the Good Fight, well known in other churches, now appears with a new tune in Hymns for Home and Church, the global hymnbook of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Its 1860 text, by the Irish Anglican clergyman and poet John Monsell, takes its theme from Paul's charge to Timothy in 1 Timothy 6:12.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Apostle’s message inspires Latter-day Saints to shed online anonymity
item.description: After Elder Quentin L. Cook urged young adults in a worldwide devotional on Sunday, "Please do not hide in anonymity to say unkind or cruel things," many Latter-day Saints had swapped real names onto previously anonymous social media accounts by Monday. Among them was Bryan Summers, who runs the Acts of the Apostles account on X and wrote that "If Elder Cook says it is wise to not be anonymous, I wanna follow him." Cook tied anonymous posting to today's contention and recalled advice from the late Anti-Defamation League leader Abe Foxman, who pointed to the masked Ku Klux Klan as an example of how hidden identity can enable violence.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Democratic candidates put faith front and center on election night
item.description: Several Democrats who won on Tuesday made religion central to their victory speeches, a shift from cycles in which faith was more often a Republican campaign feature and Democrats leaned on the religiously unaffiliated "nones." Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton, the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Kansas in 94 years, recited the Golden Rule with his crowd, and Texas Senate winner James Talarico cast his defeat of Ken Paxton as David against Goliath: "You were my slingshot." Manzhos also notes victories by Lutheran minister Sarah Trone Garriott in Iowa, Abdul El-Sayed as the first Muslim elected to the Senate, and Jewish Democrats including Brad Lander, Josh Shapiro and JB Pritzker.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: Latter-day Saints in Edmonton gather thousands of pounds of food for families in need
item.description: Edmonton's Food Bank was the main beneficiary of this fall's Latter-day Saint food drive, which wrapped up Sept. 19 with more than 257,000 pounds collected in the city and another 137,000 pounds from nearby communities. Church members in and around Edmonton have run the weeklong drive for 17 years, doing the legwork themselves.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Make giving and serving part of who you are now, Bishop Douglas tells BYU–Idaho students
item.description: BYU–Idaho students were told at a Nov. 3 devotional that they need not wait for more free time or money before helping others, as Bishop Sean Douglas, second counselor in the Presiding Bishopric, put it: "We give now when we are young with very little, so that we will always give." He pointed to humanitarian efforts of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints as examples of the kind of care for others he hoped students would carry through life.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: What to know about the Children and Youth program refinements
item.description: A Church News question-and-answer guide is meant to help parents, leaders and members with the January 2027 changes to the Children and Youth program, which The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced Nov. 3. The program, launched in 2020, has been built on gospel learning, service and activities, and personal development, and its new Youth Tool Kit and Parent and Leader guide are already in the Gospel Library app.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ announces refinements to Children and Youth program
item.description: Starting in January 2027, the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints will organize its Children and Youth program around Believe, Belong and Become, retiring the current guidebooks and dropping goal-setting built on the four areas of growth in Luke 2:52. Children starting the year they turn 8 will set one monthly goal from a new fast-Sunday Primary lesson, and Valiant-age children will share what they learned at a year-end Celebration of Growth, while youth will act on one monthly invitation from the For the Strength of Youth guide. Priests and Gatherers of Light will take on more responsibility, including teaching younger youth and planning a new Celebration of Lifelong Discipleship, and activities, camps and conferences will continue.
item.dc:creator: Mary Richards

item.title: Binge-watch this docuseries ahead of the Salt Lake Temple open house
item.description: The first five episodes of Dedicate, a Latter-day Saint docuseries tied to next spring's Salt Lake Temple open house, can now be streamed together after weekly releases that began Oct. 4, with a sixth and final episode due once the renovation is complete. The series follows seven young adults from different countries as they explore the temple and its restoration and voice doubts and questions about temple worship, and Young Women General President Emily Belle Freeman said "Nothing was scripted." Elder Gary E. Stevenson said the series was made for the rising generation and that young people "can binge-watch (these episodes) if they want to."
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: The puzzling signs of religion among young adults
item.description: A Pew Research Center analysis found that 41% of Americans ages 18 to 22 attend religious services at least monthly, above the 33% of all adults and well above the 27% of those ages 23 to 26, though the youngest group is less likely to pray daily than the overall population. Pew's Chip Rotolo said the findings send mixed signals, and political scientist Ryan Burge said college-age people may "mimic the religiosity of their parents," while Pew notes its sample of 443 carries a margin of error of about 5.7 points. Researchers warn against calling it a revival because today's youngest adults are no more religious than their peers in 2014, and although young men now report attending more than young women, Burge said the idea that men have become more religious is "just not true."
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: For these interfaith ‘poll chaplains,’ voting is a ‘spiritual task’
item.description: More than 1,000 poll chaplains organized by the nonpartisan, interfaith Faiths United to Save Democracy, joined this year by lay peacekeepers, are stationed outside polling places in nine states with contentious races to offer encouragement, practical help such as language or wheelchair assistance, and de-escalation regardless of voters' politics. The effort draws on the Black church's civil rights-era defense of the ballot, and organizer Barbara Williams-Skinner said protecting voters is a moral issue rather than a political one, and volunteers completed 90-minute trainings and will report violations to the Election Protection Group. Arizona co-lead the Rev. Dontá McGilvery, a Baptist pastor who helped recruit about 300 volunteers, called voting "our spiritual task," and Texas lead the Rev. L. Robin Murray pointed to the recent closure of 92 polling places in Tarrant County.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ leaders dedicate new temples in Mexico, Kansas
item.description: Elder Dale G. Renlund dedicated the San Luis Potosí Mexico Temple and Elder Patrick Kearon dedicated the Wichita Kansas Temple on Sunday, the church's 228th and 229th dedicated temples and the first in Kansas. Elder Renlund said what makes a temple special is not the building but "the people who come and make covenants and then keep them," while in Wichita members such as Dorothy Lawrence, whose husband of 43 years died before the temple was completed, described the day as deeply personal. The church now counts 385 temples dedicated, under construction or planned, and Mexico's 16th dedicated temple, in Torreón, is set for Nov. 22.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Jensen and Scott Taylor

item.title: Tanner McKee’s mission to Brazil gets national airtime during Eagles-Commanders game
item.description: NBC's Sunday Night Football broadcast of the Eagles-Commanders game showed photos from Philadelphia quarterback Tanner McKee's Latter-day Saint mission in Brazil, taken for a 2019 Deseret News story, as announcer Mike Tirico described him learning Portuguese. Tirico, who misidentified the faith's name, said missions "lay the spiritual foundation that you can lean into through challenges that come in life." McKee, a former Stanford sixth-round pick, has started three straight losses in place of injured Jalen Hurts, and coach Nick Sirianni said Monday the team is sticking with him.
item.dc:creator: Krysyan Edler

item.title: A first look inside Texas’ newest Latter-day Saint temple
item.description: The Fort Worth Texas Temple, the church's sixth in Texas, opened to the media Monday ahead of free public tours Monday through Saturday from Nov. 5 to Nov. 21, with dedication planned for January 2027. The roughly 30,000-square-foot, single-story building sits on 9.37 acres in Burleson, south of Fort Worth, and will be the second operating temple in the Dallas-Fort Worth area. Its design draws on the region's Spanish Colonial architecture, with Spanish lace and quatrefoil patterns, and its original art includes Matthew Grant's "Texas Bluebonnets and Longhorn Cattle."
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Watch: Why President Dallin H. Oaks has rarely missed a family reunion in 85 years
item.description: In a Church News podcast episode filmed at a family cabin, President Dallin H. Oaks and Sister Kristen M. Oaks told editor Ryan Jensen about the Olsen family reunion he first attended at about 10, when his father had died, his mother was seriously ill and he was living with his grandparents. Roughly 85 years later he still rarely misses the gathering, held every other Fourth of July weekend at the family ranch in Utah's Joe's Valley, and said "our church doctrine is rooted in the concept of family." The couple urged families to build simple, consistent traditions, with President Oaks advising, "Have a place where you always gather."
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Be lights to the world, avoid spiritual camouflage, Elder Cook tells young adults
item.description: Speaking to young adults, Elder Quentin L. Cook recalled learning of President John F. Kennedy's 1963 assassination while in Stanford's law library, followed by years of assassinations, riots and a spreading drug culture. He and Sister Mary Cook were in their 20s during that unrest, which the Church News says in some ways mirrors today's contention, and faced the same choice today's young adults face about letting their light shine through the darkness.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Where the Day of the Dead and Latter-day Saint belief intersect
item.description: In a new Spanish-language video filmed at a cemetery in Oaxaca, Mexico, Elder Neil L. Andersen of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles linked the Day of the Dead, a tradition of more than 3,000 years in which families build ofrendas and decorate graves to welcome departed loved ones, with Latter-day Saint teachings on eternal families. "There is something deeply sacred about remembering," he said, inviting members to honor ancestors by finding their names and taking them to the temple to receive ordinances. The article also notes the faith's belief that all people will be resurrected and points readers to FamilySearch's Honor Their Memory campaign.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: New ebook tells the story of Joseph Smith’s faith and financial sacrifice
item.description: The Church Historian's Press has released a Joseph Smith Papers ebook that draws on more than seven years of editing and nearly 2,000 financial documents, from store ledgers to promissory notes, to explain how the prophet financed the early Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Volume editor Sharalyn D. Howcroft said debt was unavoidable in a nation with no central bank or uniform currency, and that without it "there would be no temple," with Joseph Smith personally shouldering obligations so even the poorest Saints had a place to live. She also pointed to the Book of the Law of the Lord, a Nauvoo Temple donation record listing thousands of ordinary members, as evidence of "the sacrifice of the average member."
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Church donates and distributes 200,000 fruit trees throughout Kenya
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints gave nearly 200,000 fruit tree seedlings across 10 Kenyan counties in October, part of a six-year, roughly 600,000-seedling effort supporting a national push against deforestation and food insecurity. Elder Gérald Caussé planted a tree at the Nairobi Arboretum on Oct. 19 in support of the initiative.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Pope Leo tells global faith leaders: ‘There is no such thing as a holy war’
item.description: In a video message to faith leaders at the International Meeting for Peace in Assisi, marking 40 years since Pope John Paul II's first World Day of Prayer for Peace, Pope Leo XIV declared, "There is no such thing as a holy war: Only peace is holy." Still recovering from lung surgery, Leo said globalization had provoked fundamentalist and nationalist reactions rather than peace, and he rejected war as "an instrument of national politics" and the accumulation of arms. The article contrasts his remarks with religious justifications for war from the Russian Orthodox Church, Iranian and U.S. officials, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
item.dc:creator: Ariel Harmer

item.title: In defense of BYU’s backup quarterback, not that his post about Christ’s Atonement needed it
item.description: In the ChurchBeat newsletter, Tad Walch defends BYU backup quarterback Treyson Bourguet, a Lutheran, whose post after a loss to UCF likened the disciples' wait between Good Friday and Easter to not losing faith in the middle of a hard stretch, drawing "tone deaf" and blasphemy charges from some Utah fan accounts. Walch argues the post is reverent typology that treats Christ as the source of hope in everyday setbacks rather than equating football with the sacred. Walch frames it as an example of BYU's mission to pair faith and learning, closing on Bourguet's comment that the program has "brought me closer to Christ."
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch
